Painted around 1913 using watercolor and wash on paper, 'Journey's End' by Abanindranath Tagore is universally recognized as one of the supreme masterpieces of pathos (Karuna Rasa) in modern world art. The painting depicts an overburdened, exhausted camel collapsing onto stony desert ground at sunset. Strained to the point of death by an unbearable bundle of cargo tied tightly to its back, the animal slumps forward on its front knees, its long neck stretched out painfully and its mouth half-open, gasping for breath. In the background, a dramatic sunset burns with dusky red, ochre, and mauve tones, fading into the dark blue of approaching night. Abanindranath used his signature wash technique—repeatedly soaking the paper in water—to create a weeping, diffused twilight mist that envelops the dying creature, elevating the scene into a timeless universal allegory of exploited human labor and mortal death, conserved in the NGMA, New Delhi.

Sculpted in 1958 in bronze, 'Cries Un-heard' by Amar Nath Sehgal is a searing monument to human suffering and the trauma of the 1947 Partition of India. Having witnessed the horrific communal butchery, refugee flight, and butchered trains in Punjab during Partition, Sehgal channeled his anguish into sculpture. In 'Cries Un-heard', three elongated, emaciated bronze figures (a father, mother, and child) throw their heads back and thrust their attenuated arms toward the heavens in an agonizing, silent scream against cruelty. Beyond his art, Sehgal fought an epic 13-year legal battle against the Government of India (Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India, 2005) after his monumental 140-foot bronze mural at Vigyan Bhavan was carelessly dismantled and damaged during renovations. The landmark Delhi High Court judgment upheld Section 57 of the Indian Copyright Act, establishing that an artist possesses inalienable 'Moral Rights' (integrity and paternity) to protect their creation from mutilation, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.

Painted in 1912 by master artist Nandalal Bose using watercolor and tempera on paper, 'Parthasarthi' (Charioteer of Partha) is a defining masterpiece of modern Indian mythological art. Set in the apocalyptic prelude to the Kurukshetra war from the Mahabharata, the painting portrays Lord Krishna acting as the divine charioteer for the Pandava warrior Arjuna. Krishna is depicted at the front of the war chariot, holding the reins of four spirited white horses with his left hand while raising and blowing the sacred conch shell Panchajanya with his right hand to declare the righteous battle. His celestial face radiates divine composure and majestic authority. Seated reverently behind Krishna in the chariot is warrior prince Arjuna, his mighty bow Gandiva resting beside him, gazing with complete faith and surrender at his divine charioteer. Nandalal uses sweeping calligraphic contours influenced by the Ajanta cave murals to create an atmosphere of heroic righteousness and cosmic destiny, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.
